newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia landmine images to be posted on Internet.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia landmine images to be posted on Internet.

text.p: Acclaimed British photographer Tim Page on Sunday will start documenting the destruction of Cambodia's mine-fields to help highlight an international conference on mines.

Four of Page's images will be uploaded onto the internet home page of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to coincide with next week's Canadian government-sponsored conference, ICRC spokesman Kim Gordon-Bates said late on Friday.

The Ottawa conference "Towards a Global Ban on Anti-Personnel Landmines" will gather nearly all of the 43 countries that have unilaterally supported a global ban on the production, stockpiling, transfer and use of anti-personnel landmines.
The campaign is a first for the ICRC, which has shied away from advocacy efforts.
"This is the first time the institution has gone public on an issue," Gordon-Bates said, adding that the impetus came from ICRC medical teams weary of contending with the grisly damage done by mines.
"It was a mutiny from our own surgeons...who said we could not go forward unless we took some kind of ethical stance."
For Page, a well-known war photographer who was injured by a mine in Vietnam in 1969, the campaign has personal significance.
"When I come back here, I'm terrified," he told the Foreign Correspondents Club of Cambodia. "To take pictures of people with their limbs blown away, everyday it gets more difficult."

Page said his photographic campaign, which begins in the northwest province of Battambang on Sunday, would mark the first time images had been used on the Internet to advocate the anti-landmine cause.

Cambodia has drafted a law banning the use and purchase of anti-personnel landmines, but the legislation has languished within the government and is unlikely to be passed soon, according to ICRC officials.
There are an estimated four to six million landmines in Cambodia, making the war-ravaged country one of the most heavily mined in the world.
